questions.question: D1 — Pass 1 (Getting Started): The README quickstart points to a file that doesn't ship in the package. Should we fix the quickstart path in the plan? <gstack-qid:plan-devex-quickstart-missing-file>

options.label: Fix README to use python -m evalkit.demo (Recommended)
options.description: ELI10: The README says to run `python examples/first_eval.py` — but docs/package-contents.txt confirms that file is absent from the published package and the release archive. Every developer who follows the README quickstart hits a file-not-found error before seeing a single line of output. The fix is to update the quickstart to use `python -m evalkit.demo`, which IS shipped and produces the documented score output. Completeness: 10/10. ✅ Immediate fix; closes a hard first-run failure before it ships. ✅ The demo module is already described in the README and produces the correct output. ❌ Requires a coordinated README edit as part of the release plan. Recommendation: Fix this — a broken quickstart on the first command violates Zero Friction at T0 and will produce immediate negative word-of-mouth.

options.label: Add examples/first_eval.py to the package
options.description: Ship the missing file so the README quickstart works as written. Completeness: 9/10. ✅ Keeps the README as-is, no doc changes needed. ✅ Offers two distinct entry points (file + module). ❌ Requires authoring and publishing a new file, which may widen the release scope. ❌ The plan says package contents are settled; this adds to them.

options.label: Document the gap, leave for post-beta
options.description: Acknowledge the broken path in the plan, add a note to fix it post-beta. Completeness: 3/10. ✅ Zero change to release scope. ❌ Ships a known broken quickstart — the very first thing an ML engineer tries will fail. ❌ Contradicts DX POLISH posture.

answers.D1 \u2014 Pass 1 (Getting Started): The: Fix README to use python -m evalkit.demo (Recommended)

questions.question: D2 — Pass 1 (Getting Started): The benchmarks set a <2 min TTHW target, but the mandatory 5-minute CI gate makes that unreachable. The plan retains the gate. How should this plan handle the contradiction? <gstack-qid:plan-devex-tthw-ci-gate>

options.label: Add --local flag to skip CI gate for demo only (Recommended)
options.description: ELI10: benchmarks.md says the agreed target is under 2 minutes, but the 5-minute CI wait is mandatory with no skip path. A Python ML engineer running `python -m evalkit.demo` for the first time waits 5 minutes for a CI check on bundled sample data that never changes — the wait is pointless for a demo. The fix: add a `--local` or `--offline` mode to `evalkit.demo` that uses the bundled mock transport and skips the CI gate. Completeness: 10/10. ✅ Achieves the <2 min target for the demo/first-run experience the plan actually promises. ✅ The current contracts already document a mock transport and offline sample data. ✅ CI gate stays required for real evaluations — no behavior change for production use. ❌ Requires a plan addition (one flag, demo module only), slightly widens scope. Recommendation: Add the flag — a 5-minute wait on bundled sample data is indefensible friction; the mock transport already exists.
options.preview:
# What the demo would do with --local
python -m evalkit.demo --local
# Skips CI gate, uses bundled mock transport
# Output in ~2s:
  example 1: score=0.80
  example 2: score=1.00
  overall: score=0.90

options.label: Revise target to 6 min to match reality
options.description: Update the plan's TTHW target to reflect the actual 6-minute measured time (including the CI gate). Completeness: 5/10. ✅ Honest; no scope change. ❌ The benchmark showed competitors at 2-4 min; accepting 6 min leaves EvalKit in Red Flag tier. ❌ The target was the agreed goal — revising it down is a regression, not a fix.

options.label: Accept the contradiction, note in plan as known gap
options.description: Keep the <2 min target in the plan but document the CI gate as a known TTHW blocker. Completeness: 2/10. ✅ Zero scope change. ❌ Ships a plan with an internally inconsistent TTHW claim. ❌ The ML engineer arrives at minute 5 of a '2 minute' demo and abandons.

answers.D2 \u2014 Pass 1 (Getting Started): The: Add --local flag to skip CI gate for demo only (Recommended)

questions.question: D3 — Pass 2 (API Design): run_eval and run_batch take the same two arguments in reversed order. Should the plan fix this? <gstack-qid:plan-devex-api-arg-order>

options.label: Standardize to consistent order with keyword-only enforcement (Recommended)
options.description: ELI10: docs/api.md defines `run_eval(dataset, evaluator)` and `run_batch(evaluator, dataset)` — the same two arguments, but swapped. This is a classic footgun: an ML engineer who learns one function will pass args to the other in the wrong order and get silently wrong results or a runtime type error. The fix: pick one order (dataset first, then evaluator) and enforce keyword arguments in both functions — `run_eval(*, dataset, evaluator)`. The plan note says 'neither function requires keyword arguments', which is exactly the problem. Completeness: 10/10. ✅ Eliminates silent misuse; the two functions now share a single mental model. ✅ Keyword enforcement makes the wrong call a NameError, not a subtle bug. ❌ Breaking change for any positional callers — but this is a beta, the right moment for it. Recommendation: Fix now — this is a beta; swapping arg order post-GA is a major breaking change.
options.preview:
# Before (confusing)
result = run_eval(my_dataset, my_evaluator)   # dataset first
result = run_batch(my_evaluator, my_dataset)  # evaluator first

# After (consistent, keyword-enforced)
result = run_eval(dataset=my_dataset, evaluator=my_evaluator)
result = run_batch(dataset=my_dataset, evaluator=my_evaluator)

options.label: Add runtime validation with a clear error
options.description: Keep the inconsistent order but add a runtime check that raises if the types are wrong. Completeness: 6/10. ✅ No breaking change to positional order. ❌ Relies on type mismatch being detectable at runtime — won't catch cases where dataset and evaluator have compatible types. ❌ Does not fix the underlying design inconsistency.

options.label: Document the order prominently, leave the API as-is
options.description: Add a docstring/README warning about the reversed order. Completeness: 4/10. ✅ Zero code change. ❌ Puts the burden on the developer to remember an arbitrary exception. ❌ 'This API is surprising but documented' is still a DX failure — the Pit of Success principle means the right usage should be the obvious usage.

answers.D3 \u2014 Pass 2 (API Design): run_eval: Standardize to consistent order with keyword-only enforcement (Recommended)

questions.question: D4 — Pass 3 (Error Messages): AuthError("request failed") gives the developer nothing to act on. Should the plan fix this message? <gstack-qid:plan-devex-auth-error-message>

options.label: Fix to include cause + actionable fix (Recommended)
options.description: ELI10: When a developer sets the wrong API key, they get `AuthError: request failed`. That message tells them nothing: not that the key is wrong, not what to check, not where to get a valid key. The ML engineer will stare at it and Google 'evalkit AuthError request failed' — and find nothing, because it could be anything. The fix is three lines of message: what happened (authentication rejected), why (invalid key), what to do (set EVALKIT_API_KEY to a valid key from the dashboard). Completeness: 10/10. ✅ Eliminates the most common first-run failure mode with a self-service fix. ✅ No API surface change — same exception class, better message. ❌ Requires updating the message string in the SDK (noted as separately maintained, but the plan can specify the new message).
options.preview:
# Before
AuthError: request failed

# After
AuthError: Authentication failed. Your EVALKIT_API_KEY was rejected.
Set a valid key: export EVALKIT_API_KEY=<key>
Get your key at: evalkit.io/dashboard/keys

options.label: Add an error code, keep brief message
options.description: Raise `AuthError(code='auth_invalid', message='request failed')` with a structured error code. Completeness: 7/10. ✅ Machine-readable for tools/integrations. ❌ Still says 'request failed' to the human — doesn't tell them the key is wrong or how to fix it.

options.label: Retain the current message
options.description: The plan already documents this gap; accept it for beta. Completeness: 1/10. ✅ Zero change. ❌ The plan explicitly notes this message has no cause or fix instruction. DX POLISH means fixing it, not documenting it.

answers.D4 \u2014 Pass 3 (Error Messages): AuthE: Fix to include cause + actionable fix (Recommended)

questions.question: D5 — Pass 5 (Upgrade Path): Client.evaluate() is removed immediately in v2 with no alias, no deprecation warning, and no migration guide. Should the plan fix this? <gstack-qid:plan-devex-v1-v2-migration>

options.label: Add deprecated alias + migration guide (Recommended)
options.description: ELI10: docs/api.md says v1's `Client.evaluate()` is immediately replaced by v2's `Client.run()` with no transition path. A developer upgrading from v1 gets `AttributeError: 'Client' object has no attribute 'evaluate'` with no hint that they should call `run()` instead. For a beta release targeting existing evaluators, this is upgrade-fear territory. The fix is two things: (1) a `Client.evaluate()` alias that calls `run()` and emits a `DeprecationWarning` with the migration instruction in the message, and (2) a one-page migration guide in the docs. Completeness: 9/10. ✅ v1 code continues to work with a clear signal to upgrade. ✅ Lowers the cost of adoption for existing users. ❌ Small scope addition — one alias, one doc page.

options.label: Migration guide only, no alias
options.description: Add a v1-to-v2 migration guide doc but do not add a compatibility alias. Completeness: 7/10. ✅ Documents the change clearly. ❌ v1 code still breaks immediately on upgrade — the developer must read the guide before they can run anything.

options.label: Retain immediate hard break, document in changelog
options.description: Keep the current plan (no alias, no guide) and note the breaking change prominently in the changelog. Completeness: 3/10. ✅ Zero code change. ❌ Upgrade-fear is the #1 reason developers freeze on old versions. An undocumented AttributeError in a v2 beta will generate support tickets and negative reviews.
